scope: Controlled first-response schema failure, followed by one real DeepSeek corrective generation. Same five visible phrases with synthetic IDs and simplified metadata. No database, browser login, Mission creation or Gemini qualification.

candidates.title: Market Entry Strategy Meeting
candidates.setting: A mid-sized consumer goods company's strategy room. You are presenting a proposal for entering a new regional market to the head of business development.
candidates.goal: Convince the head of business development that the new region offers a viable entry point, clarify what you meant in your earlier written proposal, and agree on a long-term evaluation approach.
candidates.user_role: Junior strategy analyst pitching a market entry plan
candidates.ai_role: Skeptical head of business development who asks probing questions

targets.communicative_function: Identifying a specific point of entry that gives a secure initial position
targets.fit_reason: The scenario is about entering a new market, so naming the initial secure position is central to the pitch.
targets.trigger_question: Where exactly in this new region should we start so that we gain a secure initial position before competitors arrive?
targets.skip_when: Skip if the conversation has already settled on a specific entry point and moved on to pricing.

targets.communicative_function: Clarifying an indirect reference made earlier without naming it directly
targets.fit_reason: The AI counterpart can ask what the analyst meant by an earlier vague remark in the written proposal, prompting an indirect-reference clarification.
targets.trigger_question: In your memo you mentioned certain risks without spelling them out — what exactly were you referring to there?
targets.skip_when: Skip if the memo's vague remark has already been explained clearly.

targets.communicative_function: Describing a planning approach that considers long-term effects rather than quick gains
targets.fit_reason: The meeting involves evaluating whether the plan should prioritize durable results, making this description natural.
targets.trigger_question: Should this entry plan prioritize quick returns or focus on effects that play out over many years?
targets.skip_when: Skip if the discussion has already agreed on the planning horizon.

targets.communicative_function: Referring to the leadership and management of the organization
targets.fit_reason: The analyst may naturally mention the company's leadership when justifying strategic direction.
targets.trigger_question: Who at the top of the organization would need to approve this kind of move?
targets.skip_when: Skip if the conversation never touches on who leads or manages the company.

targets.communicative_function: Describing a plan becoming reality or succeeding
targets.fit_reason: Closing a strategy pitch often involves imagining the plan succeeding, so this idiom fits naturally.
targets.trigger_question: If everything goes well over the next two years, what would success look like for this plan?
targets.skip_when: Skip if the meeting ends before any discussion of future success.

candidates.title: Quarterly Review with the Board Chair
candidates.setting: A startup's small conference room. You are the operations lead giving a quarterly update to the board chair, who wants clarity on strategy and leadership.
candidates.goal: Explain your growth strategy, clarify a vague comment from last quarter's report, and align on a long-term outlook while addressing questions about company leadership.
candidates.user_role: Operations lead reporting to the board
candidates.ai_role: Board chair pressing for specifics and long-term thinking

targets.communicative_function: Identifying a specific point of entry that gives a secure initial position
targets.fit_reason: Explaining growth strategy naturally involves naming where the company can secure its first solid position.
targets.trigger_question: In this expansion, which customer segment gives us our first secure position to build from?
targets.skip_when: Skip if the board chair has already accepted the growth plan without asking about entry points.

targets.communicative_function: Clarifying an indirect reference made earlier without naming it directly
targets.fit_reason: The board chair can ask what the operations lead meant by an oblique comment in the previous report.
targets.trigger_question: Last quarter's report hinted at something without saying it plainly — what were you getting at?
targets.skip_when: Skip if the earlier report's hint has already been clarified in this meeting.

targets.communicative_function: Describing a planning approach that considers long-term effects rather than quick gains
targets.fit_reason: Board reviews commonly contrast short-term wins with durable planning, making this description natural.
targets.trigger_question: Are we planning for quick wins this year or for results that matter over many years?
targets.skip_when: Skip if the board chair has already stated the preferred planning horizon.

targets.communicative_function: Referring to the leadership and management of the organization
targets.fit_reason: A board chair would naturally ask about who is running the company and how leadership is structured.
targets.trigger_question: How is the top leadership of the company holding up under this growth?
targets.skip_when: Skip if the review stays purely on financial figures and never mentions leadership.

targets.communicative_function: Describing a plan becoming reality or succeeding
targets.fit_reason: Board reviews often close by imagining the strategy succeeding, so this idiom can appear naturally.
targets.trigger_question: If this strategy works out, what will the company look like in three years?
targets.skip_when: Skip if the meeting ends before any forward-looking success discussion.
